messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Meet Leila, a 42-year-old South Eastern Asian woman who has been struggling to come to terms with her life-threatening illness. As a project manager, she was always in control, but her brush with death left her feeling vulnerable and powerless. The smell of antiseptic wafting from the hospital corridors still sends shivers down her spine, transporting her back to those harrowing days when her life hung in the balance. Whenever she catches a whiff of that pungent aroma, Leila's mind goes into overdrive, and she becomes convinced that she is losing her grip on reality. As she navigates her daily routine, Leila finds herself constantly monitoring her thoughts for signs of "going crazy." She tries to erase the memory of her illness from her mind, but it persists, lingering in the shadows like a specter. Her attempts to suppress these memories only seem to make them more vivid, and she often finds herself reliving the terror of those moments when her life was on the line. The cold temperature of the hospital room still sends shivers down her spine, and the sight of medical equipment like needles or drips makes her feel lightheaded. Leila's memories of her illness are fragmented and disjointed, with some moments seared into her consciousness while others remain frustratingly blank. She recalls the feeling of intense fear that gripped her as she lay in the hospital bed, but the details surrounding it are hazy. Sometimes, she experiences the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, leaving her feeling overwhelmed and disoriented. As Leila struggles to make sense of her experiences, she has come to believe that her life has been destroyed by the trauma. She feels like she has failed in her most important role as a wife and partner, unable to provide for her loved ones in the way she once did. The physical toll of her illness has left her feeling permanently damaged, and she is convinced that she will never be able to regain her former strength and vitality. Leila's negative appraisals have taken on a life of their own, perpetuating a cycle of self-doubt and fear. She is haunted by the feeling that she is no longer in control, that her body has betrayed her in some fundamental way. Her memories of the illness are tainted by these negative appraisals, making it impossible for her to recall those moments without feeling overwhelmed by emotion. As Leila navigates this complex web of emotions and memories, she finds herself drawn back into the cycle of avoidance and rumination. She avoids hospitals and medical cues at all costs, terrified of being reminded of her vulnerability. Her attempts to erase the memory of her illness only serve to reinforce her negative appraisals, creating a self-perpetuating cycle that threatens to consume her. Despite her best efforts, Leila finds herself unable to shake off the feeling of being trapped in this never-ending cycle. She is desperate for a way out, a chance to break free from the shackles of her trauma and reclaim her life. As she seeks help, Leila hopes to find a way to silence the voices of self-doubt and fear that have taken up residence in her mind, and to learn to live with the memories of her illness without being consumed by them.
